props.title: Fallen Angel

sections.content: Otto Preminger's Fallen Angel (1945) stands as a masterful noir that helped define the genre's visual style and thematic preoccupations. Following Dana Andrews as Eric Stanton, a drifter who becomes entangled with both a sultry waitress and a wealthy woman, the film exemplifies noir's fascination with moral ambiguity and doomed romance. Like Preminger's earlier Laura (1944), it features sophisticated camera movements and deep focus photography that would influence countless later noirs. The film's treatment of small-town corruption and sexual obsession aligns it with other seminal noirs like Double Indemnity (1944) and The Postman Always Rings Twice (1946).

sections.content: The film's cinematographer, Joseph LaShelle, who also shot Laura (1944), creates a world of stark contrasts and threatening shadows that perfectly capture the psychological turmoil of Andrews' character. The small-town diner setting predates similar noir environments in films like The Killers (1946) and Out of the Past (1947), establishing a template for depicting American small towns as sites of hidden corruption and dangerous desire. Linda Darnell's performance as Stella, the waitress, ranks among noir's most compelling femmes fatales, combining raw sexuality with genuine vulnerability.

Fallen Angel also showcases Preminger's signature long takes and fluid camera movements, techniques that would influence directors like Max Ophüls in Caught (1949) and Robert Siodmak in Criss Cross (1949). The film's exploration of class dynamics and social mobility connects it to contemporary noirs like Mildred Pierce (1945) and Gilda (1946), which similarly examined postwar American anxieties about wealth, status, and gender roles. sections.content: Preminger's direction in Fallen Angel represents a crucial development in noir style, bridging the gap between earlier expressionistic works like The Maltese Falcon (1941) and later, more psychologically complex noirs such as In a Lonely Place (1950). The film's use of location shooting and documentary-style elements anticipates the grittier noir style that would emerge in films like Kiss Me Deadly (1955) and Touch of Evil (1958).
